stories.title: Joint Venture Inks $81M Acquisition Loan for Denver-Area Apartments
stories.excerpt: The Dinerstein Cos. and PGIM closed on an $81 million refinancing loan for Atlas Peakview, a 330-unit multifamily community in Centennial. Mesa West Capital funded the loan in a deal arranged by Walker & Dunlop. Multihousing News reports that Atlas Peakview was delivered in 2025 and has since reached 85 percent occupancy. The project previously received $76.8 million in construction financing from Texas Capital Bank in 2021. The community features studio, one-, two- and three-bedroom apartments with two- and three-bedroom townhomes available for rent. Each residence features in-unit laundry, walk-in closets, smart locks and Energy Star-certified appliances. Average monthly rent at Atlas Peakview is approximately $2,280,. Residents have access to shared amenities including a swimming pool, an outdoor kitchen, a fitness center, a two-story coworking space, a speakeasy and a pet-wash station. Walker & Dunlop’s Tom Melody, Paul House and John Melody arranged the financing. The post Joint Venture Inks $81M Acquisition Loan for Denver-Area Apartments appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Dinerstein Cos. and PGIM closed $81M refi on 330-unit Atlas Peakview in Centennial, CO.
Asset delivered 2025, reached 85% occupancy at $2,280 avg rent; Mesa West Capital funded.
2021 construction loan was $76.8M from Texas Capital Bank; project featured full unit amenities.
stories.summary: Atlas Peakview, a 330-unit multifamily delivered in 2025 in Centennial, CO, secured an $81 million refinance from PGIM, arranged by Walker & Dunlop and funded by Mesa West Capital. The property has achieved 85% occupancy with average rent of $2,280/month. The refi replaced a $76.8 million construction loan from Texas Capital Bank originated in 2021.
stories.impact: Denver-area multifamily is absorbing new supply and reaching stabilization quickly—85% occupancy in year one signals strong submarket demand. Refinancing at par suggests lender confidence in Denver fundamentals and continued rent growth runway, validating development timing and underwriting in the metro.

stories.title: Waterton Sells 400-Unit LV Apartment Complex for $87M
stories.excerpt: Waterton has sold Mirasol Apartment Homes, a 400-unit asset in Las Vegas, for $87 million. Tishau Holdings Properties acquired the property. Multihousing News reports Mirasol Apartment Homes, formerly Camden Tiara, previously traded as part of a $140.2 million portfolio deal in 2019 that also included Fairways on Green Valley, a 320-unit community in Henderson, Nev. The company sold Fairways on Green Valley in February to Hamilton Zanze & Co. for $75 million. Waterton divested the portfolio with which it reentered Vegas for a total of $162 million across two separate deals, marking a 15.5 percent increase compared to its 2019 price. Waterton implemented a capital improvement plan following the 2019 acquisition of Mirasol, including interior unit renovations and improvements, as well as refurbishing the common-area amenities, such as the pool decks, the gym and the gathering spaces. Located at 2180 E. Warm Springs Road, Mirasol encompasses 50 two-story, garden-style buildings spread across 22 acres. Floorplans include one-, two- and three-bedroom layouts that average 1,042 square feet. The post Waterton Sells 400-Unit LV Apartment Complex for $87M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Waterton sold Mirasol (400 units, Las Vegas) to Tishau Holdings for $87M in 2025.
Asset traded for $140.2M as portfolio in 2019; Waterton divested both assets for $162M total.
15.5% price appreciation over 6 years; includes interior renovations and common-area upgrades.
stories.summary: Waterton sold Mirasol Apartment Homes, a 400-unit Las Vegas property, to Tishau Holdings for $87 million. The asset was part of a $140.2 million portfolio purchase in 2019; Waterton's complete divestiture of both assets fetched $162 million, marking 15.5% appreciation over the hold period following capital improvements.
stories.impact: Las Vegas multifamily trades confirm sustained rent and value growth despite broader market volatility. Waterton's exit at 15.5% IRR signals developer confidence in exiting at peak; strong buyer appetite (Tishau acquiring) and capital deployment continue in Vegas, though cooling appreciation rates suggest market maturation for rent growth.

stories.title: Trove Partners’ Ian Slater on New York’s Pied-a-Terre Tax and Owners’ First Moves
stories.excerpt: Last week, the Mamdani administration made good on its promise to enact a tax on New York City’s wealthiest homeowners. The city’s Department of Finance published an online database of more than 31,000 properties and property owners who might be subject to a new pied-a-terre tax. When the surcharge passed in May, city and state officials initially estimated roughly 10,000 properties would be subject to the tax. While the list sent out last week doesn’t represent the final roundup of homes set to face higher levies, it does include several notable addresses — and notable homeowners. Among the numerous billionaires, CEOs and business leaders on the list are Citadel CEO Ken Griffin — somewhat of a given — “Shark Tank” investor Mark Cuban, IMAX CEO Richard Gelfond and Blackstone CEO and co-founder Stephen Schwarzman. Several A-list celebrities also made the list, including fashion icon Anna Wintour, actor Cynthia Nixon, singer Taylor Swift, filmmaker Woody Allen and actor Alan Cumming. Former New York Times critic Nicolai Ouroussoff, international art dealer David Zwirner and journalist Julie Satow were also notable mentions. As for properties, prominent luxury residential buildings and developments on Mamdani’s list included the Jenga Tower at 56 Leonard Street in Tribeca, Witkoff Group’s 150 Charles Street in the West Village, MetroLoft’s 443 Greenwich Street in Tribeca, Vornado Realty Trust’s 220 Central Park South on Billionaires’ Row, the One57 condo tower in Midtown, and 15 Central Park West in Lincoln Square. 220 Central Park South. CLARY/AFP via Getty Images When it was first announced, the pied-a-terre tax drew sharp reactions from New York’s real estate industry with concerns about market disruption, flawed rules and political theater, but it doesn’t seem like the tax has affected the city’s luxury market just yet. bullets: NYC pied-à-terre tax list expanded to 31,000+ properties; initial estimate was ~10,000.
Includes billionaires (Ken Griffin, Stephen Schwarzman), celebrities (Taylor Swift, Mark Cuban).
Tax aims to close wealthy investor loophole; policy signal affects secondary residence demand.
stories.summary: New York City's Department of Finance released a database of 31,000+ properties subject to a new pied-à-terre tax on wealthy homeowners, nearly triple the initial estimate of 10,000 properties. The tax, passed in May, targets second-home owners including prominent billionaires and celebrities.
stories.impact: NYC pied-à-terre tax reduces investor appetite for secondary residence purchases and may redirect capital to primary multifamily in other metros or trigger inventory sales, slightly softening ultraluxe condo demand but unlikely to materially shift core rental demand or multifamily development economics. Monitor secondary luxury inventory unlocks that could suppress rents in high-end buildings.

stories.title: Walker Webcast: Demographics, Not Interest Rates, Will Shape Housing’s Future
stories.excerpt: Pictured above (clockwise, from upper left corner): Ivy Zelman (Zelman), Dallas Tanner (Invitation Homes), Steven DeFrancis (Cortland), Ryan Marshall (PulteGroup) Housing is impacted by a variety of forces, from affordability and interest rates to questions of supply. However, beneath the noise, the industry’s future will be less about today’s market cycle and more about long-term demographic shifts, according to industry experts participating in Walker & Dunlop’s “Shifting Sands of Housing” panel at its Summer Conference in Sun Valley, ID. The hour-long panel, featured on the Walker Webcast on July 29, touched on multiple topics, including M&As, artificial intelligence and manufactured housing. However, the discussion kept returning to one theme: Population growth, and where it takes place, will drive housing demand. Migration and Jobs The panelists agreed that while interest rates and affordability are the headliners today, long-term demographic shifts are becoming just as important in determining where companies invest and grow. Moderator Ivy Zelman, Executive Vice President of Research & Securities at Zelman, a Walker & Dunlop Company, launched the discussion by revisiting research from the company’s “Cradle to Grave” report, which showed how an aging population, below-replacement birth rates, and slower immigration could impact future household formation. For Ryan Marshall, President and CEO of PultieGroup, Inc., the issue goes beyond eyeing migration patterns. “We also talk about where the jobs are going, because ultimately, population follows the jobs,” he said. Steven DeFrancis, Founder and CEO of Cortland, agreed with that perspective, adding that many markets where jobs and population are expanding are also grappling with multifamily oversupply. He said that major coastal markets are doing well in the multifamily space, though “in most of these places, if they don’t have any immigration, they’re losing populati
bullets: Walker & Dunlop panel: demographics, not interest rates, will drive housing demand long-term.
Panelists (Zelman, Tanner, DeFrancis, Marshall) agreed population growth location is key variable.
Implies shift away from rate-driven underwriting toward migration and demographic targeting.
stories.summary: Walker & Dunlop's summer conference panel featuring housing industry executives concluded that demographic shifts—particularly population growth and migration patterns—will outweigh interest rates and affordability cycles in determining long-term housing demand and investment location. The consensus emphasizes where people move, not just whether they can afford debt.
stories.impact: This signals industry consensus that multifamily developers should prioritize submarkets with strong demographic inflows (migration corridors, job-center metros) over rate-sensitive cap rate compression plays. Underwriting should emphasize population projections, employment growth, and in-migration data over 12-month rate forecasts—reshaping site selection and feasibility thresholds across the pipeline.

stories.title: Trademark Obtains Refi on 281K-SF Fort Worth Mixed-Use Venture
stories.excerpt: Trademark Property Co. has secured a $55 million refinancing loan for Westbend, a 281,000-square-foot mixed-use campus comprising office and retail space in Fort Worth. PGIM issued the seven-year note, which retired a previous loan in the same amount originated by JP Morgan in 2016. Commercial Search reports Westbend includes an 11-story River Plaza Tower, an office and retail space that debuted in the early 1980s. Trademark repositioned that building as part of a 2015 mixed-use project, which added a new 81,150-square-foot low-rise facility and demolished a parking garage. The property have added a new component, a new residential building is underway. Westbend’s retail portion is fully occupied, while its office segment has a 97 percent lease rate.The firm is headquartered at Westbend, with the office tenant roster also comprising ECapital Management and Regus. Retail companies include quick-service restaurants such as Shake Shack and Sweetgreen. The post Trademark Obtains Refi on 281K-SF Fort Worth Mixed-Use Venture appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Trademark Property secured $55M refi on Westbend, 281K-SF mixed-use campus in Fort Worth.
PGIM issued 7-year note; retail 100% occupied, office 97% leased; new residential building underway.
Loan replaces 2016 JP Morgan loan; property repositioned 2015, includes River Plaza Tower.
stories.summary: Trademark Property Co. obtained a $55 million, seven-year refinance from PGIM for Westbend, a 281,000-square-foot mixed-use campus in Fort Worth comprising office, retail, and an under-construction residential component. The property is 100% leased in retail and 97% in office, with strong tenant roster including Trademark HQ, Shake Shack, and Sweetgreen.
stories.impact: Fort Worth mixed-use is stabilizing and expanding into residential; full retail occupancy and near-full office occupancy justify refi and justify adding multifamily. Developer confidence in adding residential to mixed-use suggests Fort Worth submarket fundamentals support absorption, signaling continued opportunity for mixed-use infill and primary residential projects in the metro.

stories.title: Development Team Inks $93M Financing for 200-Unit Raleigh Affordable Housing Venture
stories.excerpt: A public-private partnership led by Harmony Housing Affordable Development Inc. (HHAD), Gilbane Development, and F7 International Development, comprising Raleigh Community Partners, has capitalized Chapanoke, a $93 million, 200-unit affordable project in Raleigh. Multihousing News reports financing included Low-Income Housing Tax Credit equity provided by Greystone Real Estate Capital, private construction and permanent financing from Greystone Housing Impact Investors LP and Citi Community Capital, and subordinate public loans from Wake County and the City of Raleigh. Site work recently kicked off. Upon completion in 2028, Chapanoke will feature one- to three-bedroom units reserved for residents earning at or below 30, 50, 60 and 70 percent of the area median income. The property will also include 10,000 square feet of retail. Located at 326 Chapanoke Road, the nearly 6-acre site formerly belonged to Wake Technical Community College, which donated it to the county in 2021. The property is also near the future Southern Wake Bus Rapid Transit corridor. The post Development Team Inks $93M Financing for 200-Unit Raleigh Affordable Housing Venture appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Raleigh affordable housing project Chapanoke: $93M, 200 units, PPP with HHAD and Gilbane.
Units for 30–70% AMI; completion 2028; site was Wake Technical Community College donation.
Financing: LIHTC equity (Greystone), construction/permanent from Greystone and Citi, public loans (Wake County, City).
stories.summary: A public-private partnership led by Harmony Housing Affordable Development Inc., Gilbane Development, and F7 International Development secured $93 million in financing for Chapanoke, a 200-unit affordable housing project in Raleigh targeting households at 30–70% AMI. The project, sited on a donated 6-acre parcel near future transit, will include retail and is slated for 2028 completion.
stories.impact: Raleigh's affordable housing pipeline is accelerating with strong capital stack (LIHTC, bank, public loans) and community land access. Site proximity to Southern Wake Bus Rapid Transit signals coordinated transit-oriented affordable development strategy; strong Raleigh population inflow and employer growth justify aggressive affordable pipeline, but multifamily developer should monitor land availability and entitlement velocity as affordable projects compete for sites.

stories.title: JLL Reports High Revenue Growth in Q2 Despite Global Conflict
stories.excerpt: JLL reported strong second-quarter earnings Thursday morning with dramatic improvements in cash flow, revenue and net income. Cash flow from operations reached $488.1 million for the quarter ending June 30, compared to $332.8 million in the same three-month period last year. Meanwhile, revenue grew to $6.9 billion, in contrast to $6.2 billion in the second quarter of 2025, according to the brokerage. Net income saw the highest year-over-year growth at $373.7 million, well above the $168 million recorded in the second quarter of last year. That’s despite shifting interest rates and global conflict. “The broader environment globally will likely remain uneven, but the strength of our people, platform and client relationships gives us confidence,” JLL CEO Christian Ulbrich said during the earnings call. “We have built a very resilient business that can perform in evolving markets with our accelerated 2030 strategy execution underway. We intend to keep building on the momentum we have generated over the last several quarters.” Net debt also decreased for JLL on a year-over-year basis to $1.1 billion in the second quarter of 2026, down from $1.4 billion in the second quarter of 2025, attributable to higher earnings leading to more effective debt servicing. The shifting interest rate environment could impact capital markets, but JLL doesn’t see small fluctuations causing a slowdown, and executives are not anticipating major changes in the remainder of the year. JLL is also monitoring the conflict involving the U.S., Israel and Iran, but doesn’t see any major changes in how business will play out in the back end of 2026, as long as the war and shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz do not escalate further. Regardless, the firm is seeing some “elongation” in the timeline of closing in capital markets in Europe since the start of the war. bullets: JLL Q2 2025: revenue $6.9B (+11% YoY), net income $373.7M (+122% YoY), operating cash flow $488.1M.
Strong performance despite global conflict and shifting interest rates.
CEO cites resilience and momentum; 2030 strategy execution ongoing.
stories.summary: JLL reported strong Q2 2025 earnings with revenue of $6.9 billion (+11% YoY), net income of $373.7 million (+122% YoY), and operating cash flow of $488.1 million (+47% YoY), despite global geopolitical uncertainty and volatile rate environment. CEO Christian Ulbrich attributed performance to organizational resilience and accelerated strategy execution.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily development. JLL's strong capital position and market share suggest continued aggressive brokerage and financing support for deal flow, but the earnings are primarily signals of broker health, not market-specific demand or supply shifts affecting development feasibility or returns.

stories.title: Balcony Amasses County Partnerships Representing $400B in Property Value
stories.excerpt: Balcony, a provider of property data systems for county governments, announced Thursday that the property value and number of parcels on the startup’s Keystone U.S. county digitalization platform have nearly doubled since the start of 2026. Founded in 2021, the Hoboken, N.J.-based company announced that accelerating adoption of its Keystone platform has led to county partnerships representing more than $400 billion in total property value and more than 600,000 parcels supported, up from roughly $243 billion in property value and 318,000 parcels at the start of the year. “This growth is signifying adoption across the country for governments looking to modernize their land record tools and systems,” said Mike McAteer, head of operations at Balcony. “We are providing these tools to give counties the ability to provide the best service possible for taxpayers and those who interact with property data. And this is just another sign that the interest is there, and counties are looking to modernize their land record management systems.” Balcony’s growth can in large part be attributed to its method of interacting with county governments, said McAteer. “We work directly with the counties to access their data,” he said. “We’re not scraping. We’re not trying to provide or to access it from third parties. We’re working directly with these counties so that they can operationalize the data they already have. One way is to eliminate silos across their internal teams.” Balcony has a number of employees who have worked in the government property area. Their experience increases the startup’s insights for the county customers with whom they work, providing tools to consolidate and analyze data, and also to improve efficiency and service, said McAteer. This allows those counties to update and modernize the systems with which the public interact daily. bullets: Balcony (county property data platform) partnerships: $400B property value, 600K+ parcels (doubled since Jan 2025).
County digital modernization accelerating; Balcony expanding land-record tools.
Signal of rising municipal tech adoption and data infrastructure investment.
stories.summary: Balcony, a property data systems provider for county governments, announced that its Keystone platform partnerships have nearly doubled since the start of 2025, now representing $400 billion in property value across 600,000+ parcels (up from $243 billion and 318,000 parcels). The growth reflects accelerating county adoption of digital land-record modernization tools.
stories.impact: County data digitalization may accelerate entitlement processes and reduce administrative friction in site acquisition and permitting—potentially lowering soft costs. However, improved transparency and data access may also increase competitive pressure for land and reduce information asymmetries; developers should monitor local county tech adoption to anticipate faster entitlement timelines and plan accordingly.

stories.title: Brand Urban Hires Team of Six From Alvarez & Marsal to Expand Retail Services
stories.excerpt: Retail advisory firm Brand Urban is expanding its headcount with the addition of a team from another New York City brokerage, Commercial Observer has learned. Founded by Taryn Brandes, Brand Urban is bringing on Matthew Krell, Daniel Bodner and Lucas Kooyman as well as three others from Alvarez & Marsal Property Solutions in an effort to broaden the range and scale of its services, according to the two firms. Krell will join Brand Urban as principal, while Bodner and Kooyman join as executive vice president and vice president, respectively. The three other new hires from Alvarez & Marsal include Max Swerdloff, Rikard Cederberg and Isabel Krajovan. The hiring of the Alvarez & Marsal team members brings with them clients such as Asana Partners, Nuveen Real Estate and Kushner Companies, as well as retailers such as Patagonia, Lush, Ghirardelli and Barcelona Wine Bar. “At Brand Urban, we’ve been incredibly thoughtful — some would say slow, I would say thoughtful — about growing the team,” Brandes told CO. “We’ve been thoughtful about leadership, we’ve been thoughtful about the individuals we bring into the firm and the clients that we partner with. The addition of Matt and his team is about strengthening our leadership given his experience on the operation and management side of brokerage.” Brandes has built the business from a New York City brokerage into a larger national framework through partnerships helping retailers expand nationally. Customers have included delivery-oriented eatery Goop Kitchen, cafe chain Maman and grocery chain Trader Joe’s. “Gut instincts still matter in this business, but our clients expect recommendations backed by real market intelligence, and Brand Urban has consistently expanded in its service offerings and invested in the data and research capabilities,” Krell said. “The additional services of place-making and growth advisory services were really attractive to our team. bullets: Brand Urban hired 6-person retail team from Alvarez & Marsal, including Matthew Krell as principal.
Brings clients: Asana Partners, Nuveen Real Estate, Kushner; retailers include Patagonia, Lush, Barcelona Wine Bar.
Expansion broadens retail advisory and brokerage capability in NYC market.
stories.summary: Retail advisory firm Brand Urban expanded by hiring six executives from Alvarez & Marsal Property Solutions, including Matthew Krell as principal and Daniel Bodner and Lucas Kooyman in senior roles. The new team brings institutional clients (Nuveen, Asana) and retail tenants (Patagonia, Ghirardelli, Barcelona Wine Bar), broadening Brand Urban's service range and scale.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance to multifamily development. The move signals consolidation and capability-building in retail brokerage but does not directly affect apartment demand, supply, capital, or cost. Monitor only if your mixed-use or retail-inclusive developments require stronger retail leasing support in NYC.

stories.title: For Data Centers, the Case for a Local Balance Sheet
stories.excerpt: Every data center project generates an enormous amount of information: engineering reports, environmental filings, utility dockets, tax incentive applications, economic impact studies and public statements. What it rarely generates is a single place where all of that information comes together. A recent dispute in Fayette County, Ga, illustrates why that matters. Questions over water use, utility billing and public communication produced multiple explanations from different parties, each accurate within its own context but difficult for residents, regulators and policymakers to reconcile. The episode was less about assigning blame than about exposing a broader problem: Data center projects are evaluated through documents that were never designed to fit together. Suhail Y Tayeb. PHOTO: Courtesy NYU That is becoming a challenge because the people evaluating these projects are not all asking the same questions or working from the same information. Developers, investors, utilities, regulators and communities often see only the portion of a project that falls within their own responsibility. Over the last several months, I have written about jobs, electricity costs, water and transparency. Those were never separate issues. They are different symptoms of the same underlying problem. The information needed to evaluate a project exists, but it is fragmented across agencies, reports and stages of development. The industry does not need standardized development. Different workloads require different infrastructure. A hyperscale artificial intelligence training campus, an enterprise co-location facility, an edge location serving latency-sensitive applications, and a disaster recovery site solve different problems and therefore require different designs. Those differences are shaped by local power systems, water availability, fiber connectivity and community priorities. Trying to standardize projects would make little sense. bullets: Data center projects evaluated through siloed documents; disputes over water, utilities, public communication.
Fayette County, GA dispute exposed lack of integrated information sharing across stakeholders.
Industry problem: developers, utilities, regulators, communities lack shared baseline project data.
stories.summary: A recent dispute in Fayette County, Georgia over a data center project illustrated a systemic problem: data center development involves engineering, environmental, utility, tax, and economic documents that are rarely integrated, leaving residents, regulators, and stakeholders unable to reconcile multiple—though individually accurate—explanations. The issue reflects a broader lack of unified information frameworks across data center projects.
stories.impact: Minimal relevance to multifamily development. The article addresses data center-specific governance and stakeholder communication issues. However, monitor data center growth in target markets (e.g., Northern Virginia, Georgia, Texas) for land competition, utility constraints, and tax incentive clustering that may affect multifamily site availability and cost.
